title: Objective-C runtime, KVO and interop
summary: Objective-C decides which method to call at runtime by sending messages. That flexibility enables KVO, method swizzling and associated objects, and Swift talks to it through `@objc` and bridging headers.
body: **In simple words:** In Objective-C, `[obj doThing]` sends a message "doThing" and the runtime looks up the method at that moment. Because the lookup is dynamic, you can even swap implementations at runtime.

**Message lookup:** method cache → class method list → superclass chain → if not found, forwarding (`resolveInstanceMethod`, `forwardingTargetForSelector`, `forwardInvocation`) → crash "unrecognized selector sent to instance".

**KVC / KVO:** Key-Value Coding reads/writes properties by string key (`value(forKey:)`). Key-Value Observing notifies you when a property changes. In Swift, KVO needs an `NSObject` subclass and `@objc dynamic` properties; use the block-based `observe(\.property)` API and keep the returned token.

**Swizzling:** exchanging two method implementations (e.g. to log every `viewDidAppear`). Used by analytics and crash SDKs. Risky: order-dependent, conflicts between SDKs, can break with OS updates. Prefer explicit hooks in your own code.

**Interop:** Swift sees ObjC through the bridging header (app) or module map (framework). ObjC sees Swift through the generated `ModuleName-Swift.h` for `@objc` members. Nullability annotations (`nullable`, `nonnull`) decide if Swift sees optionals; `NS_SWIFT_NAME` renames APIs; `NS_SWIFT_UI_ACTOR` / `NS_SWIFT_SENDABLE` help Swift 6.
keyPoints: ObjC uses dynamic message sending (`objc_msgSend`) with a method cache.
KVO in Swift needs `@objc dynamic` on an NSObject subclass; keep the observation token.
Swizzling is powerful but risky; prefer explicit hooks.
Bridging header (ObjC → Swift) and generated `-Swift.h` (Swift → ObjC).
Add nullability annotations so Swift gets correct optionals.

code.caption: Block-based KVO

mistakes: Not keeping the KVO token (observation stops immediately).
Swizzling in `+initialize` or without `dispatch_once`-style protection, causing double swaps.
followups: **What is "unrecognized selector sent to instance"?** A message was sent to an object that does not implement it and nothing forwarded it.
**What are associated objects?** A way to attach stored values to objects in ObjC categories / Swift extensions via `objc_setAssociatedObject`.
